newsitem.title: BRAZIL: "Revisory" session answer to Brazil's reform woes.
newsitem.headline: "Revisory" session answer to Brazil's reform woes.

text.p: Brazil's government, increasingly frustrated with its failure to get key reforms through Congress, may be tempted to call a special, "revisory" session of parliament after the 1998 elections, analysts said.

In a revisory session, the constitution can be altered with a simple majority in each house of Congress, far easier to get than the two three-fifths majorities usually needed in the fractious, multi-party Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate.
"If the government really wants to reform the civil service and the pension system then the answer could be a revisory Congress," said Ricardo Pedreira of consultants Santa Fe Ideias.

When speaking on-the-record, party leaders and presidential spokesmen say the government is too busy to consider other options while it still wages its two-year battle to get Congress approval for its civil service and pension reform bills.

But already several draft bills calling for a revisory session have been drawn up and are ready for voting in Congress, including one from deputy Inocencio Oliveira, the powerful leader of the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL).

"The government has been having a hard time, principally because of those three-fifths majorities" said Tereza Cruvinel, a columnist with newsapaper O Globo. "It can't say anything now about holding a revisory session because Congress would give up reform altogether. But it's a topic under discussion."

Brazil held a revisory session in 1993 as stipulated by the 1988 constitution. But with the country still reeling from the toppling of former president Fernando Collor and Congress riven by another big corruption scandal, no major change to the constitution was approved.

Presidential and congressional elections are due to be held in October 1998. President Fernando Henrique Cardoso is widely considered as favourite to win re-election and may call a revisory session to coincide with the first year of his second term, Congress-watchers said.

"There's a strong chance (of that)," said deputy Jose Carlos Aleluia, a reform-minded member of the PFL. "It's clear that next year's elections are going to make it hard for real reform to be approved by the current Congress, however hard it works."

The government's priorities in a revisory session would be deeper reforms of the civil service and the pensions system, Aleluia said. A long-awaited tax reform and a shake-up of the political system to reduce the number of political parties, both of which face stiff opposition, could also be included.
Other Congress-watchers say new, more competitive labor laws could be other items on the agenda.
To hold a revisory session, however, the government must first approve a constitutional amendment to that end in Congress, requiring the customary three-fifths majorities.
Rules for next year's election have to be approved in Congress by October. Any decision by the government on a whether or not it will seek to hold revisory session is expected to be made by then.

Some observers warned the move could also backfire on the government. By making constitutional amendments easier to approve, the opposition might succeed in winning some of its own, particularly in the area of labor law, political consultant Alexandre Barros said.
"It would be a risky game," Barros said. "Instead of taking things out of the constiutution, Congress might decide instead to put more in."
